genZNote: The toxin isn't even the bacterium's own gene — it's a phage's. No phage, no diphtheria, no matter how many Chinese-letter clusters you see.

habitat.hostAssociation: Strictly human pathogen/carrier; no significant animal reservoir
habitat.reservoir: Human respiratory tract and skin (asymptomatic carriers)

microscopy.stain: Gram stain; Albert's or Neisser's stain for metachromatic (volutin) granules
microscopy.appearance: Gram-positive pleomorphic rods with metachromatic granules
microscopy.arrangement: Palisades, V- and L-shaped ("Chinese letter") pairs

culture.media: Loeffler's serum slope, tellurite agar (Tinsdale medium)
culture.growthCharacteristics: Facultative anaerobe; grows well on enriched media
culture.colonyMorphology: Black/gray colonies on tellurite agar due to tellurite reduction

diseases: Myocarditis and neuropathy from toxin dissemination
virulenceFactors: Diphtheria exotoxin (encoded by lysogenic corynebacteriophage beta, tox gene) — inhibits protein synthesis via ADP-ribosylation of EF-2
clinicalImportance.transmission: Respiratory droplets; direct contact with skin lesions in cutaneous disease
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Rare where DTaP/Td vaccination is widespread; outbreaks occur in under-vaccinated populations
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Toxin production (not the organism itself) determines pathogenicity — confirmed by the Elek immunodiffusion test or PCR for the tox gene

examFacts.importantTest: Elek test; Albert's stain for metachromatic granules
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Exotoxin encoded by a lysogenic phage — only toxigenic (phage-infected) strains cause diphtheria
